# sysutils_journald_config (Resource)

Manages a systemd-journald drop-in, `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/<name>.conf`, below the provider's `root_dir` if that is set, with settings of the `[Journal]` section of `journald.conf(5)`. The file is written atomically with mode `0644`, owned by the user running Terraform (root), under the provider's shared-file lock, and is removed on destroy. Settings that are not set are not written, so the defaults and other drop-ins apply to them; drop-ins are read in the order of their names, and a later one wins. journald reads its configuration only when it starts: set `restart` to restart it when the file changes. Requires root privileges, unless used with `root_dir` on a tree you can write.

Each resource owns one drop-in, `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/<name>.conf`. The stock `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` is left alone: package upgrades may replace it, but never a drop-in.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Keep the journal on disk, capped at 1 GiB and one month, and restart
# journald so that it applies the settings right away. Writes
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/90-retention.conf.
resource "sysutils_journald_config" "retention" {
  name              = "90-retention"
  storage           = "persistent"
  system_max_use    = "1G"
  max_retention_sec = "1month"
  compress          = true
  forward_to_syslog = false

  # Other settings of the [Journal] section of journald.conf(5).
  extra = {
    RateLimitIntervalSec = "30s"
    RateLimitBurst       = "10000"
  }

  restart = true
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the drop-in without the `.conf` suffix, such as `"90-hardening"`. Must consist of letters, digits and `_.+@-`, and must not start with `.`, `+` or `-`. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `compress` (Boolean) `Compress=`: whether to compress large journal entries. Use `extra` for a size threshold instead of a boolean.
- `extra` (Map of String) Other settings of the `[Journal]` section, by name, such as `{ RateLimitBurst = "10000", MaxFileSec = "1week" }`. They are written after the typed settings, sorted by name. Names must be capitalised setting names; values must be single lines without leading or trailing white space and must not end with a backslash. A key of a typed attribute that is set, such as `Storage` with `storage`, is an error; unset, the key can hold a value the typed attribute can't, such as `Compress = "64K"`. journald ignores names it does not know, with a warning in its log.
- `forward_to_syslog` (Boolean) `ForwardToSyslog=`: whether to forward log messages to a traditional syslog daemon.
- `max_retention_sec` (String) `MaxRetentionSec=`: the longest time to keep journal entries, as a systemd time span such as `"1month"`, `"2weeks"` or `"36h"`; `"0"` turns time-based removal off.
- `restart` (Boolean) Whether to run `systemctl restart systemd-journald.service` after the file was created, changed or removed, so that journald applies it. Needs systemd to run the host, which is checked when planning, and cannot be used with `root_dir`. If the restart fails, apply fails, and the next apply writes the file and restarts journald again. Defaults to `false`.
- `storage` (String) `Storage=`: where to store the journal. `"persistent"` keeps it on disk in `/var/log/journal`, `"volatile"` in memory only, `"auto"` on disk if `/var/log/journal` exists, and `"none"` drops all logs (forwarding still works).
- `system_max_use` (String) `SystemMaxUse=`: how much disk space the persistent journal may use, as a size with an optional suffix K, M, G, T, P or E (base 1024), such as `"500M"`.

### Read-Only

- `content` (String) The rendered file. Refresh reads the file, so any change made outside Terraform shows up as a planned change to this attribute, which apply reverts.
- `group` (String) Group of the file; the primary group of the user running Terraform after apply. A different group on disk shows up as drift.
- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).
- `mode` (String) Mode of the file; always `"0644"` after apply. A different mode on disk shows up as drift.
- `owner` (String) Owner of the file; the user running Terraform (`"root"`) after apply. A different owner on disk shows up as drift.
- `path` (String) Path of the file, `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/<name>.conf`.

## The Drop-in File

The example above writes:

```
# Managed by Terraform (sysutils_journald_config). Manual changes will be reverted.
[Journal]
Storage=persistent
SystemMaxUse=1G
MaxRetentionSec=1month
Compress=yes
ForwardToSyslog=no
RateLimitBurst=10000
RateLimitIntervalSec=30s
```

- The typed settings come first, in the order above, then `extra`, sorted by name. Booleans are written as `yes` and `no`.
- A setting that is not set is not written, so the compiled-in default or another drop-in applies. journald reads `journald.conf`, then the drop-ins of `/etc`, `/run` and `/usr/lib` in the order of their file names, and a later assignment wins. Choose `name` accordingly, such as `90-...` to override a distribution's `50-...`.
- A key of a typed attribute that is set can't also be in `extra`. While the typed attribute is unset, `extra` can give the key a value the attribute can't hold, such as `Compress = "64K"` (compress entries larger than 64 KiB).
- The file is written with mode `0644` and owned by the user running Terraform. A missing `journald.conf.d` is created with mode `0755`.

## Validation

When Terraform plans:

- `name` must consist of letters, digits and `_.+@-`, must not start with `.`, `+` or `-`, and must not end with `.conf`, which is appended.
- `storage` must be `volatile`, `persistent`, `auto` or `none`; `system_max_use` a size such as `500M` or `2G`; `max_retention_sec` a systemd time span such as `1month`, `2weeks`, `36h` or `1d 12h`, or `0`.
- Keys of `extra` must look like the settings of `journald.conf(5)`: a capital letter followed by letters and digits. Values must be single lines without leading or trailing white space, and must not end with a backslash, which would continue the line. journald ignores settings it does not know, with a warning in its own log, so check the spelling of the keys against the `journald.conf(5)` of the oldest systemd you run.

## Restarting journald

journald reads its configuration only when it starts. With `restart = true`, the provider runs `systemctl restart systemd-journald.service`:

- after creating the file,
- after an update that changed the file's content, including drift that the update repaired, but not after an update of `restart` alone,
- and after destroying the resource.

Whether systemd runs the host is checked when Terraform plans, so `restart = true` fails the plan in a container without systemd, on a host booted with OpenRC, and with the provider's `root_dir`. If the restart fails, apply fails after the file was written. After a failed create, Terraform replaces the tainted resource on the next apply; after a failed update, the provider remembers the pending restart in its private state, and the next plan shows an update that restarts journald again.

On current systemd versions services keep logging across the restart: systemd holds journald's sockets, and journald keeps the services' output streams in its file descriptor store. Messages logged during the restart are queued, not lost.

## Behavior

- **Create** refuses a file that already exists. Import it instead.
- **Update** rewrites the file.
- **Destroy** removes the file. A symlink at the file is never written through or removed.

Writes are atomic and hold the provider's [shared-file lock](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/blechschmidt/sysutils/latest/docs#concurrency-and-locking), as with the other drop-in resources. With the provider's `root_dir` set, the file is `<root_dir>/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/<name>.conf`, and `path` shows the path inside the tree.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the file. Any change to its content shows up in the plan as a change to `content`, as does a change of its mode or ownership, and the next apply writes the file again (and restarts journald with `restart = true`). A file removed outside Terraform is created again.

## Import

A drop-in can be imported by its name, without the `.conf` suffix:

```shell
# By the name of the drop-in in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d, without the
# ".conf" suffix. Its [Journal] settings are read into the attributes.
terraform import sysutils_journald_config.retention 90-retention
```

The `[Journal]` settings are read into the attributes: the typed ones where their value fits, all others into `extra`. Files with other sections are refused. `restart` is `false` after import. Comments and formatting are not kept, so the first apply after an import rewrites the file in the resource's format, starting with its header comment.
